scenes.label: Lake Room diversity
scenes.line: The largest species diversity and density within the cave is found within the Lake Room. The Lake Room contains many species of millipedes, isopods, and water scorpions, likely due to the presence of oxygen in the chamber.
scenes.image_prompt: A wide subterranean chamber containing a calm underground lake reflecting rock walls., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Oxygen absent chambers
scenes.line: In contrast, primarily isopods like Caucasonethes vandeli pygmaeus and Armadillidium tabacarui are found in oxygen absent chambers. Such geological isolation is what sustains a chemosynthesis-based ecosystem, which is unique.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep dark recess of a sealed limestone cave completely devoid of flowing water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Distinct Habitat
scenes.line: The Movile Cave represents a distinct habitat that shelters a multidisciplinary community of microbial eukaryotes adapted to very specific low-oxygen, high-sulfide, and methane-saturated environments. Their significance in ecosystem stability is as a result of their communities and association with chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea.
scenes.image_prompt: dark subterranean cave chamber with mineral formations, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Groundwater System
scenes.line: The Movile Cave's unique groundwater system supports a complex community of chemoautotrophic primary producers. The different rooms of the cave have distinctive chemo-physiological conditions, allowing for the cultivation of unique bacterial genera in each environment.
scenes.image_prompt: subterranean pool of still water inside a cavern, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Bacterial Biofilms
scenes.line: The surface waters and most of the cave walls are covered in varying sizes of bacterial biofilms ranging from small, white floating patches in the Lake Room and Air-bell I to yellowish biofilms up to 2 cm thick found in Air-bell II. Because of differing atmospheric conditions throughout the cave, the sizes and community compositions of biofilms differ significantly by location, resulting in metabolically related microbial communities forming at specific cave sites.
scenes.image_prompt: close up of textured organic biofilm on damp rock, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Preliminary Studies
scenes.line: Preliminary studies of cave microbial mats revealed metabolically active methylotrophs and sulfur oxidizers, suggesting a lithotrophy-dominated ecosystem. Kumaseran et al. discovered the representative species Ca. Methylomas sp. LWB in microbial mats, presenting evidence for aerobic methylotrophy in the cave.
scenes.image_prompt: underwater microbial mat on dark sediment, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Complex Groups
scenes.line: Similar studies by Aerts et al. found complex groups of unique genera in biofilm samples collected at 3 sub-locations. Samples were taken from floating surface biofilms in Air-bell II, wall biofilms in Air-bell II, and submerged biofilms on rocks below Air-Bell I.
scenes.image_prompt: glass sample tubes resting on a stainless steel rack, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Aquimonas Genus
scenes.line: The identified microbial community from those samples are dominated by unique chemoautotrophic genera including Aquimonas which promotes denitrification and acts as a keystone genus to determine biofilm stability. Methylophilaceae functions as a methanol and methylamine reducer within the biofilm community.
scenes.image_prompt: microscope lens focused on glowing fluorescent slide, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Rhodomicrobium Bacteria
scenes.line: Rhodomicrobium are iron oxidizing purple non-sulfur bacteria, using HS- as an alternate electron acceptor. Woodsholea is a halophilic bacteria found in the Air-bell II wall biofilm with unclear metabolism.
scenes.image_prompt: purplish bacterial culture in a clear glass flask, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Nitrospiraceae Genus
scenes.line: Nitrospiraceae is a genus of ammonia and nitrite oxidizers located in the Air-bell I submerged biofilm. Cave lake water samples reveal an equally complex microbial ecosystem of methanotrophs and sulfur-oxidizers, providing substrates to support life for microbes and invertebrates.
scenes.image_prompt: submerged rocky surface under clear water, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Dominant Methanotrophs
scenes.line: Methanotrophic strains belonging to genera Methylomonas, Methylococcus, Methylocystis/Methylosinus were found to be dominant methanotrophs in water samples and encode key methane monooxygenase genes, pmoA and mmoX. Members of the sulfur-oxidizer genera Thiovulum were much more abundant and more metabolically active in Air-bell II than the Lake Room, but are dominant in both hypoxic and normoxic cave lake waters.
scenes.image_prompt: genetic sequencing computer monitor screen displaying data, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Thiovulum Stygium
scenes.line: The newly proposed species Ca. Thiovulum stygium is found to possess nitrate reduction operons as well as polysulfide reductase and sulfite exporter genes, suggesting its multifunctionality as an aerobic and anaerobic sulfide oxidation. Surface waters in the Lake Room had a diverse community of genera Sphingobacterium, Stenotrophomonas and Thiovirga.
scenes.image_prompt: laboratory pipettes transferring liquid between containers, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Deep Waters
scenes.line: Deep waters between Air-bell I and II had a high concentration of acidophilic species, mostly related to the genus Acinetobacter. Although Movile Cave sediments were initially thought to be mostly anoxic, recent metagenomic analyses reveal potential for microoxic sedimentary environments, primarily driven by chemolithoautotrophic processes and microbial commensalism.
scenes.image_prompt: deep dark water column illuminated by a flashlight, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Gallionellaceae Family
scenes.line: High abundances of microorganisms belonging to the aerobic iron-oxidizing bacterial family Gallionellaceae were found in sediment samples, specifically members of the genera Sideroxydans and Gallionella. This discovery, along with the detection of methane monooxygenase genes, suggested the possibility of proteobacterial aerobic methylotrophy as a relevant metabolic pathway for sedimentary bacterial communities.
scenes.image_prompt: rusty iron-rich mineral deposit on wet earth, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Proximity to Lakewater
scenes.line: Sedimentary microbial communities can differ depending on their proximity to Movile Cave lakewater and cultivates microniches with varying metabolic relationships. Sulfur oxidation is found to be dominant processes in lakeside sediments, evidenced by complete pathways present in the order Thiohalomonadales and family Arcobateraceae.
scenes.image_prompt: muddy shoreline of an underground cave lake, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Hydrogen Sulfide
scenes.line: Products of sulfur respiration coupled with hydrogen sulfide were found in lake-distant samples, however a full oxidation pathway could not be metagenomically assembled. Nitrogen respiration and denitrification are also key metabolic drivers in Movile Cave sediments, though most pathways are incomplete.
scenes.image_prompt: dimly lit cavern floor with rocky formations, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ammonia Monooxygenase
scenes.line: In lake-proximal samples, genes encoding ammonia monooxygenase subunits were related to the order Methylococcales. Genes for the first and second steps of dissimilatory nitrogen reduction to ammonia were found in lake-proximal and -distal samples, and closely associated with phyla Acidobacteriota, Planctomycetota, and Gammaproteobacteria.
scenes.image_prompt: laboratory bench with molecular models, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Carbon Dioxide Fixation
scenes.line: Genes associated with methane and carbon dioxide fixation have been found at both lake-distal and lake-proximal sediments. All subunits of particulate methane monooxygenase could be encoded from genes related to the family Methylococcales, thus suggesting the potential of methanotrophy occurring in the cave.
scenes.image_prompt: scientific equipment measuring gas composition, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Chloroflexota Phylum
scenes.line: Predictive gene associations have also linked CO2 fixation processes with Chloroflexota, a phylum comprising mainly thermophiles. Micrarchaeota is identified as a phylum of acidophilic archaea studied by Kadnikov et al. in 2020.
scenes.image_prompt: warm mineral spring water emitting light steam, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Methylocella Genus
scenes.line: Methylocella is a genus of class Alphaproteobacteria comprising facultative acidophilic methanotrophs as detailed by Dedysh et al. in 2005. The order Dongiales, formerly known as family Rhodospirillaceae, is a group of non-sulfur purple bacteria studied by Baldani et al. in 2014.
scenes.image_prompt: greenish microbial growth on acidic soil, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Thiohalomonadales Order
scenes.line: Thiohalomonadales is an order of class Gammaproteobacteria comprising mainly moderate halophiles as described by Sorokin et al. in 2007. Movile Cave hosts a wide range of eukaryotic organisms such as fungi and protists, which are the key eukaryotic groups within microbial mats.
scenes.image_prompt: salt encrusted mineral formation inside a cave, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Protist Roles
scenes.line: Protists are mainly involved as decomposers and oxygen producers within the Movile cave. The most dominant eukaryotic supergroups in Movile cave include alveolates, stramenopiles, and Excavata.
scenes.image_prompt: microscopic single celled organism in water droplet, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Supergroup Abundance
scenes.line: Within these groups, Alveolata and Stramenopiles is revealed to be more abundant in microbial mats, while Excavata primarily dominated the plankton fraction of the oxygen-depleted water column. Alveolata are abundant in the microbial mats and plankton as keystone grazers in Movile cave, regulating bacterial populations and promoting organic matter turnover.
scenes.image_prompt: submerged green planktonic sample under a microscope, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Alveolate Sequences
scenes.line: Alveolate sequences found in the cave were mostly associated with ciliates, with few that belonged to phylum Apicomplexa. Within Apicomplexa, the most dominant group found were gregarines, namely Ancora spp.
scenes.image_prompt: cellular organisms swimming in a fluid sample, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Dinoflagellates and Perkinsids
scenes.line: Dinoflagellates and a small number of parasitic perkinsids were present, but not as abundant. Interestingly, some sequences were related to photosynthetic species, but considering the anoxic conditions within the cave, they may be feeding on bacteria instead.
scenes.image_prompt: microscopic flagellate organism in motion, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Classes of Ciliates
scenes.line: The majority of the alveolate sequences were spread across different classes of ciliates, with three abundant classes being Armophorea, Phyllopharyngea and Oligohymenophorea. Armophorea mainly includes ciliates that thrive in anaerobic or microenvironmental conditions, with sequences linked to anaerobic metopids and some may have parasitic lifestyles.
scenes.image_prompt: multiple microscopic ciliates under a lens, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Phyllopharyngea Class
scenes.line: A novel clade under class Phyllopharyngea was the most abundant in cave ecosystems, and represents a new possible ciliate group. The class Oligohymenophorea had the greatest diversity, having numerous genetic sequences resembling anoxic or suboxic species.
scenes.image_prompt: complex single-celled ciliate organism, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Microbial Interactions
scenes.line: These microbial interactions and specialized metabolic pathways sustain the intricate subterranean food web hidden beneath the surface. The Movile Cave stands as a self-sustaining underground world driven entirely by the power of chemosynthesis.
scenes.image_prompt: intricate web of glowing biological networks, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Stramenopiles Diversity
scenes.line: Stramenopiles found in the Movile Cave were very diverse, and clustered into three abundant groups—Bicosoecids, Labyrinthulids, and Chrysophytes. Most abundant and diverse clades found within these groups were Bicosoecids, including 156 sequences while also sharing similarities with another environmental sequence from a shallow subtropical lake.
scenes.image_prompt: An underground rock formation in a dim subterranean cavern., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Low Oxygen Adaptations
scenes.line: Consistent with the cave's low-oxygen conditions, the environmental sequences most closely related to the Movile OTUs were sourced from oxygen-deprived habitats or species that thrive in microaerophilic or anaerobic conditions. Furthermore, diatom clades such as MOV-ST-4 and MOV-ST-5 that were found along Chrysophytes, are depicted to be heterotrophic lineages that are adapted to the cave ecosystem.
scenes.image_prompt: Submerged rocky surfaces covered in dark mineral deposits., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Additional Heterotrophs
scenes.line: Additional heterotrophic groups identified include Opalomonadea and MAST-3 clades, along with saprophytic Labyrinthulids and bicosoecids all adapted to the nutrient-poor and anoxic cave environment. Excavates in the Movile Cave were very diverse, with gene sequence similarities that averaged around 70-75%.
scenes.image_prompt: A close view of mineral-stained stone inside a cave., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Stygiellidae Family
scenes.line: Most sequences were related to the Stygiellidae family, including the genera Stygiella and Velundella, mainly inhabiting anoxic, sulfide- and ammonium-rich marine environments. However, the most abundant and diverse clade, MOV-EX-3 formed a distinct lineage to jakobids, and some raised a possibility of a new jakobid family.
scenes.image_prompt: Murky water in a closed underground cavity., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Microfungal Species
scenes.line: A total of 123 microfungal species have been identified within the Movile Cave ecosystem, with a notably high occurrence of microfungal spores. Of these, 96 species were detected exclusively inside the cave.
scenes.image_prompt: Rough cave walls showing layers of ancient mineral sediment., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Dry Section Locations
scenes.line: 90 species were found in the dry sections, including 51 from cave air, 42 from cave sediments, and 41 from various substrates such as dead invertebrates, corroded cave walls, and isopod feces. Airbell II contained 28 fungal species in which 23 species were present in sediments and 9 in the floating microbial mat.
scenes.image_prompt: Cracked dry sediment covering the floor of a cavern., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Exclusive Airbell Species
scenes.line: While most fungal species were widely distributed across the cave's underground habitats, two species including an undescribed species of Aspergillus sect. Candidisa and Talaromyces ruber were found exclusively in the sediments of Airbell II, while one species was found exclusively in the microbial mat in Airbell II. Due to a lack of fungal surveys following the cave's initial discovery in 1986, it remains uncertain whether these fungi are native or were introduced through contamination by researchers.
scenes.image_prompt: A delicate floating layer of microorganisms on stagnant water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Symbiotic Dependents
scenes.line: Some organisms in Movile Cave, including some invertebrate species, are dependent on symbiotic associates with chemosynthetic microorganisms. Some species, including cave-adapted isopods and leeches directly feed on microbial biofilms via their mouths, while others host endosymbiotic bacteria in their guts which aid both digestion and nutrient absorption.
scenes.image_prompt: Small pale aquatic creatures crawling on submerged rocks., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Equilibrium Interactions
scenes.line: Resident microorganisms of Movile Cave have both mutualistic and competitive interactions that balance the ecosystem equilibrium. Mutualism is evident between certain microbial populations, mainly the chemosynthetic bacteria, with these organisms being primarily involved in nutrient cycling.
scenes.image_prompt: Complex patterns of mineral deposits on wet cave stone., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sulfur Oxidation
scenes.line: For example, the sulfur-oxidizing bacteria such as Beggiatoa and Thiobacillus oxidize hydrogen sulfide to sulfate, providing materials needed by other microbial communities. Similarly, Methanotrophic bacteria like Methylomonas oxidize methane and contribute organic carbon to heterotrophic microorganisms.
scenes.image_prompt: White bacterial filaments swaying in clear groundwater., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Food Web Foundation
scenes.line: These cooperative interactions create stable microbial mats, the high-energy foundation of the cave food web. Two species of the groundwater amphipod genus Niphargus have been observed in Movile Cave.
scenes.image_prompt: Thick microbial mats covering the bottom of an underground pool., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ectosymbiotic Relationship
scenes.line: One specimen of the species Niphargus cf. stygius found in Movile Cave was observed in an ectosymbiotic relationship with sulfur-oxidizing Thiothrix bacteria, a genus of bacteria known to thrive in inverse sulfur-oxygen gradients, and have been observed in ectosymbiotic relationships with invertebrates in hydrothermal vent locations. Thiothrix was found primarily attached to the hairs and spines on the amphipods' legs and antennae.
scenes.image_prompt: Microscopic view of bacteria attached to crustacean hair structures., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Genetic Distinction
scenes.line: These epibionts were discovered through genetic sequencing to be genetically different from the free-living Thiothrix found in microbial mats within Movile Cave, suggesting the epibionts have adapted to living on Niphargus cf. stygius. This association suggests an ecological interaction, where the bacteria may play a role in nutrient acquisition or protection against pathogens in the nutrient-poor, sulfur-rich cave environment.

scenes.label: Evolutionary Adaptations
scenes.line: The long-term isolation of Movile Cave has led to unique evolutionary adaptations of its microorganisms and eukaryotic communities. They have undergone genetic divergence in small isolated populations and established novel symbioses, such as those between invertebrates and sulphur-oxidizing bacteria.

scenes.label: Eukaryote Evolution
scenes.line: Studying these systems provides insights into the early evolution of eukaryotes with an interest in protists adapted to anoxic conditions. In this respect, Movile Cave also provides an excellent terrestrial analogue for deep-sea hydrothermal vents and extraterrestrial ecosystems, favouring the scenario of life existing subsurface beneath moons like Europa or Enceladus.
